rv.q: Its edifice is built with bricks of banality and mortar of treacle, and it melts before our eyes.
For two acts, Sherman and Hull sketch the tale in a comprehensive manner that, unfortunately, becomes repetitious.
For all its busyness, “Empire” is too often an energy-sapping exercise, its fictionalized plot so pointlessly convoluted it hardly feels worth sorting out.
But a mediocre book and lyrics make it less comparable to its steel and concrete namesake and more like a souvenir version.
Alas, that is where the value of Caroline Sherman and Robert Hull's well-meaning but clumsy show ends.
Empire is an ambitious but unsuccessful musical which is defeated by its very form.
The clumsy memory-play framework stunts the show from the start.
Its book rests on a shaky foundation, is shoddily constructed, and relies on prefabricated materials; as it stands, it doesn't even rate as a fixer-upper.
Unfortunately, the result is less inspirational.
The characters are engrossing in their struggles and desires.
In the end, Empire seems stuck in the blueprint stage — unsure what type of show it wants to be.
The major issue is that there are too many stories going on and rather than adding substance and depth, they distract.
Alas, that is not the case with the shockingly drab and clueless Empire: The Musical...

cn.t: Critics find this Empire State Building musical well-intentioned but fundamentally flawed, with muddled storytelling and uninspired execution overshadowing occasional heart and strong performances.
